summary: Looks at the shortcomings of existing localized mobility solutions, which all involve the host, and makes the case for network-based localized mobility management. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: Today phones have to help the network when they move between access points. This note argues the network should handle that itself so phones can stay simple.

questions: what is the difference between local and global mobility
why is network-based mobility management useful
subtitle: Why a moving phone should not have to run mobility software just to roam around one access network.

tldr.problem: When a mobile node moves between access routers inside one access network, existing solutions either need extra software on the host or are proprietary and tied to one kind of link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares the existing approaches, lists their shortcomings, and argues for an interoperable, network-based protocol that handles local movement without any host stack involvement.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a protocol. It makes the case for network-based localized mobility management and points to RFC 4831 for the goals.

facts.label: Problems with global mobility per move
facts.value: Update latency, signaling overhead, location privacy

today: RFC 4830 is an Informational RFC from April 2007 with no listed obsoleting or updating RFC. It frames the problem, and the goals for a solution continue in RFC 4831.

sections.title: Why Take a Fresh Look
sections.content:
The IETF had already produced experimental host-based protocols for localized mobility: Fast Handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6) and Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 (HMIPv6). Both need the host to take part at the IP layer, like Mobile IPv6 does for global mobility.

Two developments prompted a new look. First, global mobility protocols other than Mobile IPv6, such as the Host Identity Protocol (HIP) and IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming (MOBIKE), mean future wireless nodes may use a more diverse set of protocols. Second, WLAN switches already manage mobility with no host stack involvement, which suggests a paradigm that keeps host software simpler.

IPv6 and wireless links are the initial scope, though the RFC says its conclusions apply equally to IPv4 and wired links.
sections.eli5: Some ways of keeping a moving phone connected make the phone do extra jobs. New kinds of phones may do things differently, so people wanted to ask whether the network could do the job instead.

sections.title: Local, Intra-Link and Global Mobility
sections.content:
The RFC defines an access network as a collection of fixed and mobile network components giving Internet access within a single operational domain. Local mobility is movement across such an access network. It sits between two other cases:

  • Intra-link (Layer 2) mobility: moving between access points under the same access router, normally handled by Layer 2 mechanisms.
  • Local mobility: moving between two access points connected to two different access routers.
  • Global mobility: moving between two access networks, which may need a global mobility protocol such as Mobile IP, HIP or MOBIKE.

The scope excludes transitions between service providers in separate autonomous systems, and the access network is assumed to be a standard IP routed network (for example OSPF, IS-IS or RIP) with no specialized routing protocol.
sections.eli5: Moving between two wifi boxes on the same router is a small step. Moving to a whole different building's network is a big step. This note is about the in-between step.

sections.title: Problems with Global Mobility for Every Move
sections.content:
A global mobility protocol can be used between access routers, but the RFC names three well-known problems with doing that for every move:

  • Update latency: if the anchor point or correspondent node is far away, the update takes a long time, and packets sent to the old temporary address are essentially dropped meanwhile.
  • Signaling overhead: configuring an address on the new link and updating the mapping can use a lot of wireless bandwidth and hurt real-time services.
  • Location privacy: a changing temporary address exposes the node's topological location to correspondents and possibly eavesdroppers.

Localized management also gives local control and means a node need not support a global protocol for movement inside the domain, although traffic is disrupted when it leaves that domain.
sections.eli5: If every tiny step meant sending a long letter far away, the mail would be slow, wasteful and would tell strangers where you are. Handling small steps close by avoids that.

sections.title: Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC gives three settings where localized mobility management helps.

  • Large campus: a campus WLAN too spread out to be one IP subnet. WLAN switches handle this today, but their protocols are proprietary, so IP mobility requires switches from the same vendor.
  • Advanced cellular network: next-generation cellular protocols such as 802.16e could run IP deeper into the access network. An interoperable protocol could unify local mobility across cellular, WLAN, UWB and Bluetooth, complementing Layer 2 mobility.
  • Picocellular network: very short-range radio could mean node-dense networks with subnets covering a small area such as one room. Aggregating many subnets under one scheme can reduce IP signaling.
sections.eli5: A big campus, a phone network, and tiny room-sized wireless bubbles all have devices moving around a lot. A shared way to handle it would help all of them.

sections.title: Existing Solutions and the Network-Based Alternative
sections.content:
Existing solutions fall into two classes. Class 1 is interoperable IP-level protocols that change the mobile node's IP stack. Class 2 is link-specific or proprietary protocols, such as those in WLAN switches.

For class 1: requiring host stack software limits broad use, since the success of WLAN switches shows operators and users prefer no host changes; all such solutions depend on Mobile IP or derivatives, though nodes may choose HIP or MOBIKE; they do not support both IPv4 and IPv6; and host-based schemes need extra security associations with network elements in the access domain.

For class 2: they only support WLANs with Ethernet backhaul, each vendor's protocol is proprietary and does not interoperate, and being based on Layer 2 routing they may not scale to a metropolitan area or province.

The RFC concludes that an interoperable, standardized protocol that scales to topologically large networks and needs no host stack involvement is highly desirable. Compared with class 1, it requires no localized mobility support on the mobile node and is independent of the global mobility protocol, so it can be used with any or none of them. That gives a more modular architecture.

Compared with class 2, an IP-level network-based solution works for link protocols other than Ethernet and for wide area networks. The reference architecture and protocol goals are left to RFC 4831.
sections.eli5:
One kind of fix makes every phone install extra stuff. The other kind only works with one brand of equipment. Neither is great.

If the network does the work, any phone can roam without special software, and it works no matter what kind of wireless link is used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Host-based localized mobility protocols carry all the security problems of providing a service to a host. Network-based management needs security among network elements equivalent to what is needed for routing information security, and security between host and network equivalent to what is needed for network access, but no more. A fuller discussion of security goals is in RFC 4831.
sections.eli5: The network's own devices must trust each other, and your phone must prove it may join. The note says nothing more than that is needed.
